IAMA Male Elementary School Teacher. AMA.

As a child I had ADHD pretty badly. I started studying Computer Science in College but had a hard time sitting all day focusing on coding. Trying to reevaluate what I wanted to do, I thought of things that I enjoyed and was good at. Even in middle school and high school I had done lots of work with younger children (both in Boy Scouts as well as with local summer camps) and decided that I wanted to work with kids. Having ADHD has also given me valuable perspective on my students and I think has turned from a detriment in a field like Comp Sci to an asset in the field of teaching.
have you ever been hit on by a female student?
Never hit on, when I student taught with second graders there were definitely a lot of girls who were, I would say, infatuated with me. But just silly kid stuff.
The normal way I guess, found a college that had a decent program, didn't skip too many classes, passed all my exams, got degree and license, got job, got paid.
What is the weirdest thing you have seen an elementary school student do? Whether it be getting something strange or just something gross.

Oh god, kids are weird so I am so inundated with weirdness it is hard to pull a specific example that sticks out.

This year alone I had a child wear his lunchbox on his head, several kids call me dad by mistake (happens every year), had a child from another class flick boogers all over my carpet, and more that aren't coming to me at the moment.

I expect weirdness in kids, it's the weirdness of parents (no offense to any parents) that always throws me off.

I also had one parent that was just off the walls bizarre. She would say the weirdest/most inappropriate things to me and my coworkers.

The weirdest thing she did was not to me but my unmarried 30something coworker who she advised "Could have a baby without a man."
What is your favourite subject to teach? Your least favourite? Also, are the cafeteria ladies still creepy?
Social Studies. Reading. More angry than creepy.
follow up question, since working in the school system have you developed an appreciation for other positions in the school system? For example, janitorial staff, security, counsellors, etc.

I definitely have the utmost respect for the custodians, the cafeteria workers, and our tech support who often work behind the scenes and get no recognition. I rely on my counselor a lot every year and would have a hard time doing my job without her.

On the flip side, positions I have little respect for are on the more administrative side of things. The instructional coaches, the principals and assistant principals (although our AP in particular is amazing, but mainly because she actually was a classroom teacher for many years), the reading specialists and math specialists who all tend to the make the job harder.
How do you feel about standardized testing?

Standardized testing by itself is an important part of education but requires expertise to know how to interpret and properly utilize the results. Using it for evaluations of schools, teachers, and even as the sole way to evaluate students, is a mistake. There is so much that standardized testing doesn't measure at all or measures poorly for it to be used as an all important measurement tool.
If you could incorporate a new method of benchmarking the students, faculty, and school how would you?

If we wanted to stick to testing, I would have students take a test at the beginning of the year to find out what "Grade level" they truly are on (for example, this 4th grader might be reading like a 1st grader). Then they would take a similar test at the end of the year that would show their growth over the year (for my previous example, this student might pass if they made a year and a half growth in reading, even though they're not at a 4th grade level yet).

The alternative to that is a portfolio method which would also show growth over time, but having done portfolios for alternative assessments, they take a looooooong time.

I know some teachers that I find to be seriously under qualified. For example a couple whose spelling is atrocious.

As a parent I think these people should not be allowed to teach, and the level of education of teachers nowadays is sub par.

Have you encountered this in any form, and how do you feel about it?

I don't know of any programs that produce underqualified teachers. I feel universities do a good job of weeding these people out. What I see more are older teachers who have been burnt out by all the changes in the last 10 years. As to qualifications, the worst teacher I have seen is also the "highest qualified" teacher I have known. She had her National Board Certification which is partially obtained by submitting video tapes of your lessons. It is very difficult to achieve and even some of the best teachers I have known have failed due to the specifics required by it. This teacher got it by repeatedly teaching the same lesson over and over again, having her kids rehearse their answers and questions, so that when she video taped and submitted it it was "perfect."

For levels of education teachers have I would disagree. Most teachers I know have their masters degree and all teachers (in Virginia at least but I believe it is similar around the country) need to do a certain amount of professional development every 5 years in order to maintain their license.

Thanks for taking the time to answer.

Understanding your position, I wonder why kids nowadays are worse in spelling, mathematics and several other areas than kids that attended the same teachings 20 years ago. This seems to be a thing primarily in Europe and the US

What's your view on this?

The problem with this is we don't have the same kids as we did 20 years ago. If you look at the white and Asian students who did well 20 years ago, they're still doing well. It's the influx of Hispanic students who are coming from poverty and do not have the same support structures who are struggling in the current setting.

Here is a good article that breaks down how the US does when you break out districts that have certain levels of poverty and compares it against countries of a similar level: http://nasspblogs.org/principaldifference/2014/02/pisa-its-still-poverty-not-stupid/

While it is an unpopular view (even among other educators who truly believe that teachers can make up for any discrepancy at home), if we want to address the "issues" of education we also need to be addressing the issues of poverty.

How afraid are you of crazy parents suing you because they think you might be a pedo?

Has a patent ever showed distrust in you because you're a guy?

Afraid probably isn't the right word; however, it is constantly on my mind. Even a false accusation can ruin a career. The things I do is to belong to the union (in case of a false accusation they provide legal representation), make sure I am never alone with a child, and I even avoid touching a child under any circumstances (I would never literally pat a child on the back, but rather give verbal praise).

I have never had a parent show me any distrust. In fact many parents are excited to have me because I am a guy (especially the parents of boys).

I've heard that "good touching" is important for social reassurance, but in the context of mental hospitals so maybe this doesn't apply as much for kids that already feel normalized.

Do you feel like your hesitancy to give pats or other physical positive reinforcements affect the kids in a way that alienates them? What about high fives or fist bumps? Do kids ever try to give you hugs and you need to tell them no?

I'm not too sure about that, I guess I hope that their physical needs get met by their parents. I do also rely heavily on our guidance counselor when a student is in high distress and in need of consoling.

I do reciprocate hugs that are given but try to turn it into a side hug with a small pat on the back as opposed to a full on embrace. I do allow high fives and fist bumps.
That is the one I am wondering about. I have heard that male teachers in elementary schools are viewed with suspicion, which is one of the reasons there are so few of them.

In the way that a black man experiences racism that others don't readily recognize, being watched in a store or people crossing the road to put distance between them for example, do you experience behavior of others that could be accusatory of perverted or deviant traits of you? (That's about as clear and encompassing as I can make it; I hope it's understood.) If so, how does it affect your behavior and interactions - with students? - parents? - colleagues?

Also, do you find that male students behave and perform better in your classroom than with female teachers in general?

I haven't dealt with any distrust from parents, students, or colleagues due to my gender but as I said in another response, I take certain steps to remain above reproach (such as avoiding being in a room with a child alone, not touching children for any reason, etc) that my female peers don't. I will say that I am treated differently because of my gender in the social realm though. I don't often get invited to the social events that my colleagues have. Which does have its blessings (I have only been to two baby showers in my five years of teaching).

I don't believe male students behave any better, but having grown up with ADHD and still dealing with ADHD on a daily basis (which we know is more prevalently exhibited in boys), I do think I have a better perspective on dealing with them and trying to help them be successful in a different way than maybe a female teacher would.

What would you say is the most important thing kids need to learn/be taught that isn't a standard part of education? Flip side, What do you have to teach your students that you just don't think is important/is a waste of time?

How to take responsibility for their actions and interact with other people. Look at any workplace and the issues within it. Most of them are not due to people being uneducated but because people lack important social skills. This tends to be done well in the lower grades but it really is something that needs to continue throughout education. I would argue even at a collegiate level.

Cursive, I taught it every year when I taught third grade but it was mainly to fill the dead time we have the month after standardized testing takes place. I think in this day and age typing should replace it.
Followup, do you believe that there is a "correct" method of typing?
Afraid I'm not informed enough about different methods of typing than the standard way to have much of an opinion.

Do you do any kind of special activities that you enjoy in your class?

One of my elementary school teachers had us write a short book and a company actually printed all of our books out. I still have it. She seemed to enjoy everyone being astounded that our books became real.

That's pretty cool. The librarian does a writing club and many of them get poems published but I have never heard of a company that will print out a class's books for cheap.

I try to do things that I enjoy from my background. If we have time I try to work in programming using a kid friendly language (Scratch). I also do a lot of engineering projects with my kids as team building exercises as well as where I can attach them to our curriculum.
